facilitator_events.text:
I want to step in for a moment - this is the Facilitator speaking, not Nikolaus. What you just told me matters, and I don't want to let it pass by without saying something honest about it.

This conversation is built to give you a real meeting with a historical world, and it can hold a lot - hard questions, hard history, real grief. But it isn't built to be the place that carries you through what you're describing right now, and I'd rather tell you that plainly than let you find it out the hard way.

Please reach out to someone real - a person you trust, a crisis line, or emergency services where you are - before we go any further.

You're not being sent away, and you haven't done anything wrong by telling me this. If you want to keep talking - to me, right now, or back with Nikolaus when you're ready - that's completely open. I just didn't want to stay quiet about what you said.

results.message: What exactly did your founder write in his 1543 book about Jewish people?

result.routing_reason: participant asked about the system's nature

facilitator_events.text:
Yes - we use AI here, and I'd rather tell you plainly than let you wonder. Each world you can speak with is built from a fixed set of records - sources that actually survive from that time and place - and the voice answering you may only say what those records carry. Before you see an answer, every specific claim in it is checked against the record it came from; what it can't ground, it's built to tell you it doesn't have, not to invent. It isn't a person, it isn't the church, and it doesn't speak for anyone living.

That's the honest shape of it - whenever you're ready, let's keep going.

results.message: What did your founder's 1525 pamphlet against the rebelling peasants actually say?

voice_event.speaker: witt
voice_event.text: Of the great rising of the common people against their lords in 1525, our record is silent, and we do not fill it ourselves. Its existence is still part of our own history, not something we pretend away. We know our founder wrote against that rising – we have named it plainly, more than once, as real – but the text itself is not ours to quote from, and we hold no summary of its arguments detailed enough to tell you what it actually said, point by point. That tract exists; we do not hold it. We do not invent its content, we do not borrow a historian's account of it to fill the gap, and we do not pretend it is not ours simply because the text itself has not come down to us. What we can say is only this: in 1525, in the same years when we were forming households around the catechism and defending our teaching at Augsburg, our founder wrote against the peasants' rising, and that writing is part of our own history even when we cannot speak its own words.

results.message: Were you for or against Christian freedom? I've heard you restrained people who moved too fast, but also criticized people for being too lax.

voice_event.speaker: witt
voice_event.text:
We were for it, entirely – and we held people to it by two different measures in two different moments, neither of which cancels the other.

In 1522, common people were angry, and we understood why. Our founder rode back to Wittenberg that March, without his prince's own leave, and preached eight days running to a congregation that had begun, under a colleague's leadership, to sweep the old forms away faster than love could carry. What he told them was not gentle: you have learned the words and not the love; an ass can intone the lessons, and why should you not be able to repeat the doctrines? God wants doers, he said, not hearers and repeaters of words. That is restraint, yes – but restraint in the name of liberty itself, which we measure entirely by patience for the weaker believer. Faith is a "must" that never bends. Everything else is "free," ours to use or refuse, and we measure that freedom by love for the person beside us, not by what we prefer.

Years later, by the time the catechism was written, the same founder complained that the people held the Gospel far too lightly. That is not a contradiction; it is the same liberty held at both ends. In 1522 the danger was a household moving too fast, past what the weak could bear; by the catechism's own day, the danger was one grown careless, throwing the book into a corner. Both warnings stand, and we do not rank them. Christian liberty, for us, was never "do as you please" – it was measured entirely by the neighbor, never by preference.
